docs.title: QuantumEd
docs.text:
A free, open quantum computing curriculum for community learners, high school students, and undergraduates.

QuantumEd is built around interactive, visual explanations of core quantum computing concepts — not just text. Each module can be downloaded from the button at the top of the navigation pane so you can keep learning offline.

docs.title: How the curriculum is organized
docs.text: Module Focus 01 · Foundations Why quantum computing, what a qubit is, where the field stands today 02 · Quantum Computing Fundamentals Qubit representation, the Bloch sphere, gates, circuits 03 · Quantum Programming Python/Jupyter setup, Qiskit and other SDKs, running on simulators and real hardware 04 · Quantum Hardware Physical qubits, control/readout/noise, hardware modalities 05 · Quantum Software Stack Compilation, transpilation, runtime, calibration 06 · Quantum Algorithms & Methods Intro algorithms, VQE, QAOA, quantum annealing 07 · Quantum Error Correction Stabilizer and surface codes, syndrome decoding, lattice surgery 08 · Labs & Learning Modules Hands-on labs across programming, hardware, algorithms, and QEC

docs.title: Who this is for
docs.text: No prior physics or linear algebra background is assumed in Module 01. Later modules build on earlier ones, so the fastest path through is top to bottom — but each module page is self-contained enough to jump to if you already know the basics.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: QuantumEd is open source. See the repository to suggest edits or new content — every page has an "Edit this page" link.

docs.title: 01 · Foundations
docs.text: Start here if you're new to quantum computing. This module builds the vocabulary and mental models everything else in QuantumEd relies on — no linear algebra assumed going in.

docs.title: What's in this module
docs.text:
• Why Quantum Computing? — the motivation for the field, the classes of problems it targets, and how it differs from classical computing at a conceptual level.
  • What Is Quantum Computing? — qubits, superposition, measurement, and entanglement, with an interactive demo.
  • Quantum Computing Today — the NISQ era, the path to fault tolerance, and today's practical limitations.

Once you've worked through these three pages, move on to 02 · Quantum Computing Fundamentals for the math and circuit model behind the concepts introduced here.

docs.title: Qubits
docs.text:
A classical bit is always either 0 or 1. A qubit is a two-level quantum system whose state is a combination — a superposition — of both:

\[ |\psi\rangle = \cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)|0\rangle + e^{i\varphi}\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)|1\rangle \]

Any single-qubit state can be pictured as a point on the surface of a sphere — the Bloch sphere — where \(\theta\) sets how much of the state points toward \(|0\rangle\) versus \(|1\rangle\), and \(\varphi\) sets a phase that becomes important once qubits interact with each other.

Drag the sliders below to move the state around the sphere and watch how the measurement probabilities change.

θ — polar angle: 90° φ — phase angle: 0° |ψ⟩ = 0.71|0⟩ + e^{i0°}·0.71|1⟩ P(measure 0) = 50.0%    P(measure 1) = 50.0%
